cards.text: The Teacher, son of David and king in Jerusalem (Ecclesiastes 1:1), has been talking about money. He just said that when God gives a man riches and lets him enjoy them, that's a gift from God (Ecclesiastes 5:19). Now he says he's seen another evil under the sun, one that weighs heavily upon mankind.
Picture a man God gives riches, wealth and honor, so he lacks nothing his heart desires. The man's wish list is EMPTY, friend.

cards.question: This man has riches, wealth and honor, and he lacks nothing. So what's the evil the Teacher sees in it?

answers.text: God does not allow him to enjoy them
He loses all of it in one night
His honor slowly turns into shame

cards.text: Instead, a stranger will enjoy them. That's like baking a perfect batch, and while you're still hunting for the oven mitts, some guy you've NEVER MET walks in and eats every single one.

cards.question: True or false: the Teacher calls this situation futile and a grievous affliction.

cards.text: Then the Teacher goes bigger: a man may father a hundred children and live for many years. A huge family and a long life, friend.

cards.question: True or false: the Teacher says a long life and a hundred children make up for a man being unsatisfied with his prosperity.
Picture a man with a hundred children and a long life who is unsatisfied with his prosperity and doesn't even receive a proper burial. Who does the Teacher say is better off than he is?

cards.text: The Teacher says the stillborn child enters in futility and departs in darkness, and his name is shrouded in obscurity. The child never sees the sun or knows anything.

cards.question: The stillborn child never sees the sun or knows anything. But what does the Teacher say that child has more of than the unsatisfied man?

cards.text: The Teacher says the child has more rest even if the man lives a thousand years twice over but fails to enjoy his prosperity. That's TWO THOUSAND years, friend.

cards.question: True or false: after comparing the unsatisfied rich man with the stillborn child, the Teacher asks whether all go to the same place.

cards.text: Now the Teacher looks at every man's work. He says all a man's labor is for his mouth.

cards.question: The Teacher says all a man's labor is for his mouth. What does he say about that man's appetite?

answers.text: It is filled by hard work

cards.text: That's me with cookie dough: one batch and I'm DONE, then five minutes later I'm preheating the oven again. And now the Teacher starts asking hard questions.

cards.question: The Teacher starts asking hard questions. What does he ask about the wise man?

answers.text: What advantage he has over the fool
Why he keeps his wisdom hidden
Whether his name will last forever

cards.text: He also asks what gain comes to the poor man who knows how to conduct himself before others. Then he weighs what the eye can see against the wandering of desire.

cards.question: True or false: the Teacher says the wandering of desire is better than what the eye can see.

cards.text: It's the batch on the cooling rack beating the ten you keep daydreaming about. And the Teacher says this too is futile and a pursuit of the wind.
Then the Teacher says whatever exists was named long ago, and it is known what man is. Named long ago, friend, just like me, carved into my handle by the family who brought me home for a quarter.

cards.question: True or false: the Teacher says man cannot contend with one stronger than he.
Then the Teacher talks about words. He says the more words, the more futility. What does he ask right after that?

cards.text: Hoo, that one hits ME, friend, because I haven't stopped talking since the oven warmed up. Then the Teacher asks who knows what is good for a man during the few days in which he passes through his fleeting life like a shadow.

cards.question: True or false: the Teacher says he can tell a man what will come after him under the sun.
